markers.method (how operationalised from 2d phot: Rater panel; or model trained on ratings. Cues include FWHR (r = .35 with masculinity judgements in men, Geniole 2015), cheekbone prominence and longer lower face (Scheib 1999), redder/yellower sclera (Kramer 2022), lower facial contrast (Russell 2009)
markers.norms: Rating scale
markers.perception: See linked cues; Scheib 1999 linked facial masculinity to both symmetry and attractiveness

markers.name: Perceived femininity (rated)
markers.definition: Observer-rated femininity, mainly for female faces
markers.photo: Frontal, no makeup (cosmetics raise contrast and femininity)
markers.method (how operationalised from 2d phot: Rater panel or trained model. Cues: higher facial contrast (Russell 2009), whiter, less red sclera (Kramer 2022), feminine shape (Perrett 1998)
markers.norms: Rating scale
markers.perception: Raising facial contrast makes an androgynous face look female (Russell 2009)

markers.name: Facial luminance contrast
markers.definition: Luminance contrast between features (eyes, brows, lips) and surrounding skin
markers.photo: CCC, controlled light, no makeup, frontal
markers.method (how operationalised from 2d phot: Feature ROI L\* vs surrounding skin L\*, e.g. (skin−feature)/(skin+feature) (Russell 2009; Porcheron 2013)
markers.norms: Unitless. Higher in female than male faces (Russell 2009); decreases with age (Porcheron 2013). Norms: not found
markers.perception: Higher contrast → more female (Russell 2009); younger looking (Porcheron 2013); cross-cultural age cue (Porcheron 2017, Chinese and French/Caucasian samples, per title and authors)

markers.name: Facial colour contrast (a\*, b\* contrast)
markers.definition: Redness/yellowness contrast between lips/eyes and skin
markers.method (how operationalised from 2d phot: As above on a\* and b\* channels
markers.norms: Unitless. "Aspects" of contrast decrease with age (Porcheron 2013); which channels was not detailed in the abstract
markers.perception: Faces look younger when these contrasts are raised and older when lowered (Porcheron 2013)

markers.name: Neoteny / babyfaceness
markers.definition: Similarity to infant facial proportions (large eyes, small lower face, high forehead, round face)
markers.method (how operationalised from 2d phot: Rated babyfaceness; anthropometric indices (eye size relative to face, lower-face height ratio, forehead height) as in Berry & McArthur 1985 and Jones 1995
markers.norms: Rating / ratios; norms not found
markers.perception: Babyface components and their social consequences (Berry & McArthur 1985). Neoteny and female attractiveness, cross-cultural (Jones 1995). Review of appearance-based impressions (Zebrowitz & Montepare 2008). Abstracts not retrieved for Berry 1985 / Jones 1995

markers.name: Facial adiposity (perceived facial weight)
markers.definition: Perceived weight / fat in the face
markers.photo: Frontal, neutral; jawline and cheeks visible (head covering can hide the jaw outline)
markers.method (how operationalised from 2d phot: Perceived-weight ratings (Coetzee 2009); objective proxies are the three Coetzee 2010 ratios (FWHR, perimeter-to-area, cheek-to-jaw width)
markers.norms: Ratings; ratios (below)
markers.perception: Facial adiposity predicted perceived health and attractiveness and was linked to cardiovascular health and reported infections (Coetzee 2009). Review (de Jager 2018)

markers.name: Facial width-to-height ratio (FWHR)
markers.definition: Bizygomatic width ÷ upper-face height (brow or nasion to upper lip)
markers.photo: Strictly frontal, neutral, no head tilt; zygion and upper-lip landmarks visible
markers.method (how operationalised from 2d phot: Landmarks: bizygomatic width / upper-face height (Carré & McCormick 2008; Weston 2007). Component analysis in Costa 2017
markers.norms: Ratio. Meta-analysis: larger in men (d = .11, n = 10,853); r = .31 with BMI (Geniole 2015)
markers.perception: Larger FWHR judged more threatening (r = .46), more dominant (r = .20), less attractive (r = −.26), more masculine in men (r = .35) (Geniole 2015). Predicted reactive aggression in men and hockey penalty minutes (Carré & McCormick 2008)
markers.sources: Carré & McCormick 2008; Weston 2007; Geniole 2015; Costa 2017; Coetzee 2010

markers.name: Cheek-to-jaw-width ratio
markers.definition: Bizygomatic width ÷ jaw (bigonial) width
markers.method (how operationalised from 2d phot: Landmarks
markers.norms: Ratio. Linked to BMI in both sexes (Coetzee 2010)
markers.perception: Used by observers to judge weight in African and Caucasian faces (Coetzee 2010)

markers.name: Facial perimeter-to-area ratio
markers.definition: Face outline perimeter ÷ enclosed area
markers.method (how operationalised from 2d phot: Contour from landmarks / segmentation
markers.norms: Ratio. Linked to BMI in males (Coetzee 2010)
markers.perception: Used by observers to judge weight (Coetzee 2010)

markers.name: Perceived (apparent) age / youthfulness
markers.definition: Age estimated by observers from the face; "looks young for age" = perceived minus chronological age
markers.photo: Frontal (+ obliques), neutral, no makeup, CCC if colour cues used
markers.method (how operationalised from 2d phot: Rater panel age estimates (Gunn 2009; Nkengne 2008); PLS models from graded skin attributes (Nkengne 2008); AI from Skin Aging Atlas grades (Flament 2026)
markers.norms: Years; Δ vs chronological age. Flament 2026: 96–98% of AI grades within one atlas unit of experts (East Asian, African, European only)
markers.perception: Main cues: wrinkling, grey hair, lip height, sun damage (Gunn 2009); eye area, skin colour uniformity, lips (Nkengne 2008); facial contrast (Porcheron 2013, 2017); sclera colour (Russell 2014); topography more than colour (Samson 2011)
markers.sources: Gunn 2009; Nkengne 2008; Porcheron 2013; Porcheron 2017; Russell 2014; Samson 2011; Flament 2026

markers.name: Lip height (age cue)
markers.definition: Vertical height of the vermilion
markers.method (how operationalised from 2d phot: Landmark distance (vermilion borders) ÷ face height
markers.norms: Ratio; norms not found
markers.perception: Larger lips → looking younger for age; lip height mainly genetic (Gunn 2009). "Lips border definition" was a cue for older graders (Nkengne 2008)

markers.name: Perceived health (rated)
markers.definition: Observer-rated healthiness of the face
markers.method (how operationalised from 2d phot: Rater panel or model trained on ratings. Drivers to measure: skin redness/oxygenation, yellowness, homogeneity, adiposity
markers.norms: Rating scale
markers.perception: Skin blood colour (Stephen 2009a); facial skin coloration (Stephen 2009b); carotenoid/melanin colour (Stephen 2011); adiposity (Coetzee 2009); predictors of attractiveness and health (Foo 2017); averageness/symmetry vs actual health (Rhodes 2001b)
markers.sources: Stephen 2009a; Stephen 2009b; Stephen 2011; Coetzee 2009; Foo 2017; Rhodes 2001b

markers.name: First impression: trustworthiness / valence
markers.definition: First trait dimension of face evaluation
markers.photo: Neutral expression (emotion resemblance drives this), frontal
markers.method (how operationalised from 2d phot: Rated trustworthiness; data-driven shape/appearance models (Oosterhof & Todorov 2008)
markers.norms: Rating / model score
markers.perception: Valence and dominance are two orthogonal dimensions; valence is driven by expression-like features (Oosterhof & Todorov 2008). Replicated on 1,000 ambient images (Sutherland 2013)

markers.name: First impression: dominance
markers.definition: Second trait dimension (physical strength / ability to harm)
markers.method (how operationalised from 2d phot: Rated dominance; model scores; FWHR as a partial cue
markers.norms: Rating / model score
markers.perception: Dominance evaluation is sensitive to cues of physical strength (Oosterhof & Todorov 2008). FWHR → dominance judgements r = .20 (Geniole 2015)

markers.name: First impression: youthful-attractiveness
markers.definition: Third dimension found in ambient images
markers.method (how operationalised from 2d phot: Factor score from trait ratings (Sutherland 2013)
markers.norms: Factor score
markers.perception: A "youthful-attractiveness" factor emerged beside trustworthiness and dominance (Sutherland 2013)

markers.name: Overall facial attractiveness / first impression
markers.definition: Rated attractiveness
markers.photo: Frontal, neutral, no makeup; head covering affects ratings
markers.method (how operationalised from 2d phot: Rater panel; composite of averageness, symmetry, dimorphism, skin cues
markers.norms: Rating scale
markers.perception: Meta-analysis on attractiveness consensus and effects (Langlois 2000). Predictors of attractiveness and health (Foo 2017). Emirati men rated faces with fully covered heads lower; partially covered heads rated as attractive as uncovered (Jordan 2020). Emirati women's ratings by covering condition were also studied (Sheen 2018); the result is cut off in the abstract record and not verified

markers.name: Face shape class and facial proportion indices
markers.definition: Facial index (height/width) and related proportions; face-shape category (oval, round, square, heart, long)
markers.photo: Strictly frontal, hairline and jaw visible (head covering limits this)
markers.method (how operationalised from 2d phot: Anthropometric indices from landmarks (Farkas 2005 measurement set, 14 measurements); shape category by rule-based thresholds on indices. No validated face-shape classification from 2D photos found. Categories are convention, not evidence
markers.norms: Farkas 2005 gives ethnic normative ranges incl. three Middle-East groups (12.2% of n = 1,470; full text not accessed, so values not extracted)
markers.perception: Not found for shape categories
